tags.description: Sea cave on the NW corner of Kapa Island, entrance ~4.5m deep, cave floor ~18m. Faces west, so best light is in the afternoon. Schools of baitfish shelter inside from predators; hundreds of swiftlets (locally called swallows) nest in the roof. Late-1800s inscriptions are visible on the cave walls above the surface. A secondary cave/swim-through system reaches 20-21m with a very strong current possible in places.

tags.qa_note: 'Coral Garden' is a real, commonly used site-name pattern among Vava'u operators (dive-shop listings reference Coral Garden N/S sites in the area), but no source ties a site by this exact name to these exact coordinates, and no site-specific depth/marine-life report was found. Left as unvalidated; description trimmed to avoid site-specific claims that cannot be sourced.
tags.description: A reef site in the Vava'u group. Vava'u's shallow reef areas generally offer coral gardens with soft and hard coral growth, but no source-confirmed, site-specific details were found for this exact location.

Vava'u's outer walls are a well-documented diving style in the region, but no site-specific source confirms details (depth profile, marine life, conditions) for a site by this exact name at these coordinates.

tags.qa_note: Corrected misidentification: this coordinate (Neiafu Harbour, Vava'u) previously carried the name 'St Catherine Wreck' with a fabricated backstory. No source anywhere documents a 'St Catherine' wreck in Tonga. The well-documented, famous wreck at this exact location and depth is the Clan McWilliam (sunk 1927). Renamed and rewritten accordingly. Sources disagree on registered tonnage (3,743 tons vs 6,000 tons) and on the exact sinking date (Dec 24 vs Dec 25, 1927) -- both are flagged as unresolved discrepancies in the markdown rather than picked arbitrarily. Depth and difficulty updated from 25m/Intermediate to 37m/Advanced to match sourced maximum depth.
tags.description: Clan McWilliam, a copra steamer built in 1918, caught fire while loading cargo in Neiafu Harbour and sank on 24-25 December 1927. Now lies at approx. 37m max depth (superstructure ~18-29m), marked by three mooring buoys. Encrusted with hard/soft coral; home to schooling fish, batfish, snapper, small tuna, and macro/crustacean life.

tags.qa_note: Vava'u's July-October humpback whale season and outer-wall diving are both well documented destination-level facts, but no source ties a distinctly named 'Humpback Wall' site to these exact coordinates. Left as unvalidated; rewrote to separate the well-sourced destination-level whale-season facts from unconfirmed site-specific claims (removed unconfirmed marine life list).
tags.description: A wall site on an outer Vava'u island edge. Tonga's Vava'u group is one of the few places in the world with legal in-water humpback whale encounters, July through October/November, and outer walls are a common dive style in the area -- but no source confirms site-specific details for a location named 'Humpback Wall.'

tags.qa_note: Corrected fabricated eruption date: the description previously claimed a 'most recent eruption in the early 2000s.' Wikipedia, VolcanoDiscovery, and the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program all agree the last confirmed eruption was June 1957 (with unconfirmed gas/discoloration observed in 2022). No source of any kind -- dive shop, forum, or database -- documents recreational diving at Fonualei. All previously invented dive-profile, current, and marine-life content (hammerhead/manta/humpback claims) has been removed as unconfirmable. Left unvalidated.
tags.description: Fonualei is an uninhabited active volcanic island approx. 70km northwest of Vava'u, rising 1,000m from the seafloor with a 2km diameter and 188m max height. Its last confirmed eruption was in June 1957 (an earlier major eruption in 1846 devastated Vava'u's vegetation with ashfall). No dive operator, forum, or database documents recreational diving here; whether this is an actively dived site could not be confirmed.

tags.qa_note: Corrected: shallow entrance is ~3m (snorkel-accessible), deeper diver entrance is ~12m, not '1-4m/12-15m' as previously stated. Corrected the naming legend -- multiple sources describe a rebel chief hiding a forbidden love interest in the cave for months before escaping with her to Fiji, not simply 'protecting her from an arranged marriage.' Depth field updated from 15m to 12m to match the sourced diver entrance/wall-dive profile.
tags.description: Underwater cave on the west side of Nuapapu Island. Shallow entrance ~3m deep (snorkel-accessible); a second, deeper entrance around 12m is used by divers. Incoming swell compresses air in the chamber, producing a brief 'fog-out' each time a swell passes. A lobster is regularly seen near the 12m (40ft) swim-through. Exiting and turning left leads to a wall dive with two further swim-throughs around 6-12m. Named for William Mariner, a young English clerk who survived the 1806 massacre of the crew of the Port-au-Prince and lived in Tonga for about four years; local legend holds that a rebel chief hid a forbidden love interest in the cave for months before escaping with her to Fiji.

tags.qa_note: Renamed from the generic 'Eua Island' to the actual named dive site, Cathedral Cave. Removed a significant fabrication: the previous description claimed 'Eua has no commercial dive operators and requires private charter logistics. In fact, Deep Blue Diving (based in the Tongatapu/'Eua area, run by Sam Tatafu, a retired Tongan Navy officer) is a known, active operator running trips to this exact cave. Rewrote entry/exit, safety, and overview sections accordingly.
tags.description: Cathedral Cave, discovered circa 2001 on 'Eua's north coast, is a sea cave roughly 100m long, 50m wide, 30m deep, with the entrance at 28m. Three openings in the roof let sunlight stream in; a 20m tunnel leads to a second chamber near the surface. Marine life recorded here includes sharks, groupers, and schooling reef fish (cardinalfish, butterflyfish, sweetlips) along healthy coral. Deep Blue Diving runs guided trips to this site; diving/snorkelling tours generally run November-June, outside Tonga's whale season.

tags.qa_note: Flagged discrepancy: the only account found describing a vessel named Takuo says it was a fishing vessel that foundered on Hakaufisi reef in the Ha'apai group during a storm, with the hull eventually washing up on Nomuka Iki -- lives were lost. This account could not be corroborated by a second independent source (direct fetch of the source page returned 403; no other outlet mentions it), and it is ambiguous whether that vessel is a diveable, tide-covered wreck (consistent with the official LINZ hydrographic chart tag 'water_level: covers' at this coordinate) or a fully beached relic. Depth/site_type left unchanged (chart data does support a real, charted, tide-covered wreck at this location) but NOT marked validated given only one uncorroborated narrative source. Removed fabricated 'coral encrustation abundant, moderate currents typical' filler that had no source.
tags.description: A charted wreck (LINZ hydrographic ID 8269138) in the Ha'apai island group, tagged as tide-covered with the hull showing. A single, uncorroborated web account describes a fishing vessel named Takuo that foundered on Hakaufisi reef in a storm, with the hull later washing ashore on nearby Nomuka Iki; this could not be independently confirmed and may describe a different remnant than the charted wreck at this position. Treat site-specific details as unconfirmed.

tags.name: My Lady Lata II Wreck
tags.qa_note: Renamed from the OSM chart label 'Marmer' (kept as alt_name) to the vessel's real, well-documented identity, My Lady Lata II -- a half-submerged wreck at Pangaimotu Island near Nuku'alofa, a popular, easily accessible snorkel/dive site. Sources conflict on the cause/date of sinking: one account (2014) attributes it to a cyclone approx. 12 years earlier (~2002); a separate account attributes wreck material at Pangaimotu to Cyclone Gita (Feb 2018). It is unclear whether both describe the same vessel; this conflict is stated explicitly in the markdown rather than resolved by guessing.
tags.description: My Lady Lata II, a half-submerged wreck at Pangaimotu Island near Nuku'alofa harbour, sits in ~2-2.4m of water and is a popular, easily accessible snorkel/dive site. Sources disagree on when and how it was wrecked -- one account attributes it to a cyclone roughly two decades ago, another associates Pangaimotu wreck material with Cyclone Gita (2018); which storm produced this specific wreck is not resolved.

tags.name: Ata
tags.qa_note: Corrected a significant misclassification: this site was tagged site_type='reef' with a description implying it is (or is near) the famous remote, uninhabited 'Ata island. It is not. Real 'Ata island is at approx. 22.34S/176.21W, about 150km from this coordinate (21.13S/175.16W, near Tongatapu's coast). Meanwhile, OSM's own source tags for this exact point say historic=wreck / seamark:type=wreck with a LINZ hydrographic wreck ID -- i.e., the official chart data itself says this is a charted shipwreck, not a natural reef. Changed site_type from reef to wreck on that basis. No source identifies the specific vessel. Left unvalidated; all previous 'pristine remote island reef' narrative content removed as unsupported/misleading.
tags.description: A charted wreck (LINZ hydrographic ID 3857295, tagged 'dangerous'/submerged) near Tongatapu, not the well-known remote, uninhabited 'Ata island roughly 150km to the south despite the shared name. Vessel identity and history could not be established from available sources; treat as an unidentified charted wreck pending further research.

tags.name: Hakau Tapu
tags.qa_note: Two independent geographic-reference sources (mapcarta.com, geographic.org) confirm this reef's real name and general location near Kanokupolu/Ha'akili on Tongatapu's coast (also charted as 'Duff Reef'), and confirm 'hakau'/'tapu' as real Tongan words meaning 'reef'/'sacred, restricted.' That falls short of the 3-independent-source bar and neither source is dive-specific (no depth, marine life, or conditions confirmed), so left unvalidated rather than padded. Removed unconfirmed dive-specific claims (visibility figures, coral/current description) that had no source.
